steps.caption: As time goes on, we are not getting farther from the text of the New Testament. We are getting closer. Here is the case, one piece of evidence at a time.
The objection: copying is a game of telephone. So copy John 1:1–5 two ways: down a single chain, and across a branching tree.
Every copy makes mistakes, a few words in every hundred, and half the copies are then lost.
Now vote, word by word, across whatever survives. The chain keeps the errors it inherited. The tree’s independent lines outvote them.
Take a single word. In the chain, every survivor inherited the same slip. In the tree, the slip is a small minority.
In 1516 Erasmus edited the Greek New Testament from a handful of copies made about a thousand years after the originals.
Watch what scholars could read as the centuries pass. Each dot is a manuscript arriving; the dashed line is the earliest one known.

steps.caption: Today the earliest fragment sits about fifty years from the original. For other ancient authors the gap is centuries, with far fewer copies.
This is P66, a papyrus book of John copied around 200 AD. It is written in capitals, with no spaces.
Follow it word by word against the Greek in a modern edition and the English under it.
With so many copies, the problem is not missing text but extra text. The disputed passages are not hidden: they are in your footnotes.
John 5:4, the angel stirring the water, is missing from the earliest manuscripts. Take it out, and the story still reads.
There are hundreds of thousands of variants. Most are spelling. About one in a hundred both changes the meaning and could be original.
Names are hard to fake. The Gospels use the common names of first-century Palestine at about the rates the population did.
And they add a second name exactly where a common name would be ambiguous: Simon called Peter, James son of Zebedee. Rare names go without.
Why does Jesus ask Philip, of all people, where to buy bread? John never says.
Luke puts the feeding near Bethsaida. John mentions, elsewhere, that Philip came from Bethsaida. Jesus asked the local.
None of this is hearsay. Thousands of manuscripts are catalogued, and hundreds can be opened page by page from the libraries that hold them.
Every piece of this has critics, and their strongest points are on the site next to each chart, with the sources. Check them.
